exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with burning urination and vaginal discharge – what key history and exam elements differentiate urethritis from vaginitis? — Look for discharge character, itching, and perform speculum exam; urethritis lacks discharge and has localized urethral erythema.

A patient with HIV on ART develops dysuria, no fever, dipstick positive for leukocytes but negative nitrite – what is your next step? — Send urine for culture; consider Enterococcus or Staphylococcus and start empiric nitrofurantoin pending results.

In a rural clinic, a man reports dysuria and hematuria; ultrasound unavailable – how do you assess for obstruction? — Estimate bladder volume by palpation, ask about post‑void sensation, and consider catheterisation to measure residual.

Why is nitrofurantoin preferred for uncomplicated cystitis in areas with high fluoroquinolone resistance? — It concentrates in urine, low systemic toxicity, and retains activity against common uropathogens.
A pregnant woman presents with dysuria; which antibiotic is safest? — Use amoxicillin or nitrofurantoin (avoid in first trimester if possible); avoid tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
What red‑flag signs would prompt immediate referral for possible pyelonephritis? — Fever >38.5 °C, flank pain, vomiting, and rising creatinine.

A male patient has dysuria and perineal pain; what condition should you consider and how does treatment differ? — Acute prostatitis; requires longer‑acting antibiotics (e.g., trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole) and may need prostate‑specific evaluation.
ai.title: Dysuria
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Painful or difficult urination signals urinary tract pathology. In low‑resource settings common causes include infections, stones, and obstructive lesions. A systematic approach to history, exam and targeted investigations guides safe management.

b: Acute symptom, may be isolated or part of a syndrome
Often the first clue to urinary infection or obstruction
sections.p: Dysuria is the symptom of pain, burning, or discomfort during voiding. It reflects irritation or inflammation of the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder neck, or bladder).

b: Urethral dysuria: often sexually transmitted infections or urethritis
Bladder dysuria: cystitis, stones, tumors, interstitial cystitis
sections.p: Classify dysuria by location (urethral vs bladder), duration (acute <2 weeks vs chronic), and associated features (frequency, urgency, hematuria, flank pain).

b: Unrecognised obstruction can lead to upper‑tract infection and renal failure
Severe pain with fever may indicate pyelonephritis, a medical emergency
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent causes are bacterial cystitis, sexually transmitted urethritis, and schistosomal cystitis. HIV‑positive patients are at higher risk for opportunistic infections and atypical presentations.
When culture is unavailable, treat empirically based on local resistance patterns and re‑evaluate if no improvement in 48 h.

t.b: Detects pyuria or bacteriuria; positive nitrite suggests Gram‑negative rods
Confirms pyuria, hematuria, crystals; guides need for culture
Identifies pathogen and antibiotic susceptibility; essential for recurrent cases
Detects chronic schistosome infection causing cystitis

b: Uncomplicated bacterial cystitis: oral nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (if local resistance <20 %). Avoid fluoroquinolones when possible due to resistance and tendon toxicity.
Stone‑related dysuria: analgesia, hydration, and referral for lithotripsy or surgery when available.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve pain, and prevent complications.

t.b: Reduces pain, improves oral intake; avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment
Increases urine flow, helps flush bacteria and small stones

b: Vulvovaginitis – presents with itching and discharge; treat with topical agents.
Prostatitis – men with perineal pain, urinary hesitancy; may need prostate‑specific antibiotics.
Interstitial cystitis – chronic pelvic pain without infection; managed with bladder training.

Urine microscopy may miss low‑grade bacteriuria if sample is delayed.

b: Ask about timing, severity, associated urinary symptoms, sexual history, and recent antibiotics.
Examine abdomen for suprapubic tenderness, bladder distension, and flank pain.
In women, perform a gentle speculum exam to rule out vaginitis.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever (>38.5 °C) with dysuria – suspect pyelonephritis
Flank pain or vomiting – possible obstructive uropathy
Gross hematuria or inability to void – urinary obstruction
